new_statements.quote: Gugu-Badhun words have a regular primary stress on the first syllable. The only exception to this is /djibíya/ = whistler duck, where, for reasons of onomatopoeia, the stress falls on the second syllable. Stems of three or more syllables usually have a secondary stress on the third syllable. Suffixes which form a third syllable do not usually take secondary stress.
new_statements.citation: Sutton, Peter John. 1973. Gugu-Badhun and its neighbours: a linguistic salvage study. MA thesis, Macquarie University, Sydney. 273 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 3 'Gugu-Badhun Phonology', section 3.2 'Word Stress', thesis p. 82 (PDF p. 83)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word; a secondary stress usually falls on the third syllable of stems of three or more syllables, but a third syllable supplied by a suffix usually carries no secondary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Usually on the third syllable of stems of three or more syllables; suffixes that form a third syllable do not usually take secondary stress. Phonetic transcriptions on pp. 80-82 mark a grave on the final vowel of trisyllables, e.g. [bálanò] 'moon', [búlaɹì] 'two'.
new_statements.exceptions: One lexical exception, /djibíya/ 'whistler duck', with stress on the second syllable, attributed to onomatopoeia.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; a phonemic 'word' in Sutton's sense (stems plus suffixes), from salvage elicitation of citation forms and short sentences with the last speakers (1970 fieldwork). Sec. 3.3 adds that words have at least two syllables and the longest observed word has seven.
new_statements.identity_note: Sutton's chapter 3 describes Gugu-Badhun proper (upper Burdekin River, informants incl. Eric Gertz and Richard Hoolihan, 1970 fieldwork) = gugu1253 / AUSTLANG Y128. He treats Warungu (warr1255) and Gudjal (gudj1237) as the other two 'Upper Burdekin River dialects'; the stress rule is stated for Gugu-Badhun only. Wikipedia and Dixon (2002) treat Gugu-Badhun as a dialect of Warrongo, but Glottolog keeps it as a separate language.
